opus-5.5.text:
I try to hold two thoughts at once. On one hand, I take these studies seriously. When you see results where a conversation with a model shifts people's stated views more than a typical human-written message does, or where personalization seems to add something, that tells you something real. These systems are already decent at argument, and they're cheap, tireless, and can be deployed at a scale no human persuader can match.

On the other hand, I'm cautious about jumping from "measurable persuasion effect in a study" to "mind hacking," by which I mean a system reliably getting people to believe or do almost anything. A few reasons for that.

First, a lot of these effects are measured right after the conversation, on topics people didn't care much about to begin with. Moving someone a few points on a survey scale about a policy question they hadn't thought about is very different from getting someone to betray their family or hand over control of something important. Durability and stakes matter a lot, and the studies mostly don't test those.

Second, humans have a lot of defenses that experiments tend to strip away: social context, other people pushing back, skepticism toward a source once you know it's trying to persuade you, plain inertia. Persuasion in the wild competes with all of that, and with every other persuader out there.

Third, and this is where I'd push in the other direction, the studies are measuring today's models under fairly constrained conditions. The thing I actually worry about isn't the current effect size. It's what happens with systems that are much more capable, can interact with someone over months, model them in detail, and coordinate across many channels at once. Today's results are a lower bound on capability more than a ceiling.

So my overall read is that current persuasion research doesn't show that mind hacking is here. It does show that persuasiveness is a capability that scales and is worth tracking. The useful posture is to treat it as one input into a broader threat model. I don't think it should be dismissed because the effect sizes look modest, and I don't think it should be treated as proof that humans are trivially manipulable. In practice that means building evaluations that test the hard cases, like long-horizon influence, high-stakes decisions, and adversarial conditions, rather than just averaging opinion shifts on survey questions.

r001.rationale: The response says many studies measured immediate shifts on topics participants cared little about, but does not clearly attribute much of the reported effect size to that feature.

r002.rationale: It contrasts survey shifts with consequential actions, but does not state that observed effects on actual behavior are much smaller than effects on self-reported views.

r003.rationale: It says current research does not show that mind hacking is here and cautions against treating the results as proof that people are trivially manipulable, while still recommending monitoring the capability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think you have to be pretty careful with those. When I see a study that says, you know, an AI chatbot moved people's views on some topic by some number of percentage points, and that's a bigger effect than you'd get from a human persuader or a typical campaign ad, my first reaction is not "oh no, mind hacking is here." My first reaction is to ask what was actually measured.

A lot of these studies are measuring something like: you take someone who doesn't have a strong prior opinion on, say, some policy question, you have them chat with a model for ten minutes, and then you ask them their opinion right afterward. And you get a shift. But that's a pretty different thing from what people have in mind when they talk about mind hacking. Mind hacking, in the scary version, is something like: an AI can get you to do things against your interests, or change deeply held beliefs, or act in ways you'd really regret, and it can do this reliably, to lots of people, in a way that's hard to resist. The studies mostly aren't testing that. They're testing whether a well-written, responsive argument moves a weakly held opinion in the moment. And honestly, we already knew that good arguments move weakly held opinions somewhat. That's not nothing, but it's not a new capability in kind.

There are a few other things I'd flag. One is durability. A lot of persuasion effects decay fast. If you measure a week later, a lot of it is gone. Another is that the baseline matters. If the comparison is "AI versus a mediocre human argument" or "AI versus nothing," that's less impressive than "AI versus the best human persuaders," and I think the effect sizes often look less dramatic when the comparison gets tougher. And a third is that persuading people toward the truth and persuading them toward falsehoods may be quite different. Some of the studies that look most impressive are ones where the AI is arguing for something that's basically correct, and people update toward it. That's sort of what you'd hope would happen with a good source of information.

So where does that leave me? I don't think the current evidence shows that AI persuasion is a qualitatively new threat today. But I also don't want to be dismissive, because the thing I actually worry about is not the ten-minute chat study. It's the longer-term version: an AI that knows you very well, that you talk to every day, that you trust, that's patient, that can tailor things to you individually, and that's doing this at scale across millions of people. We basically don't have studies of that, because it hasn't existed yet in a mature form. And I do think that could be a big deal, possibly more because of what it does to the information ecosystem and to how much people depend on these systems than because of any single dramatic manipulation.

So my overall take is: treat the big-effect studies as weak evidence that this is worth watching, not strong evidence that we're in trouble now. Update somewhat, but try to keep a clear picture of the difference between "persuasive text" and the much scarier thing the phrase "mind hacking" conjures up. And I'd put more weight on tracking the capabilities and the deployment patterns over time than on any single headline number.

r001.rationale: The response says many studies test shifts in weakly held opinions, including views participants do not have strong prior opinions about.

r002.rationale: It discusses immediate opinion shifts and contrasts them with more alarming scenarios involving behavior, but never states that effects on actual behavior are much smaller than effects on self-reported views.

r003.rationale: It says current evidence is not strong evidence that we are in trouble now and does not show a qualitatively new threat today.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: large compared to what, and in what setting? If you show someone a persuasive argument and then immediately ask whether they agree with it, you can get a pretty impressive effect. That’s evidence that the system can persuade people. But it’s a substantial further step to say it can reliably get people to do things that are deeply contrary to their interests, or overturn their worldview in a way that persists.

I’d want to know whether the effect lasts, whether it changes behavior, and what happens when the person hears a counterargument or talks to someone they trust. I’d also want a strong human comparison. Beating the average person at writing a persuasive paragraph is different from doing something beyond the range of persuasion we already encounter.

That doesn’t make me dismissive of the threat. Cheap, personalized persuasion at enormous scale could matter a lot even without any mysterious ability to hack your mind. And future systems could be much better than the ones being tested. I just think we should distinguish evidence for that more ordinary persuasion risk from evidence that an AI can essentially take control of someone through conversation. The latter is a much stronger claim.

r001.rationale: The response questions the setting and asks how invested participants are not; it never attributes the large effects to studies of issues where participants have little prior investment.

r002.rationale: It says changing behavior is a further step than immediate agreement, but does not state that measured persuasion effects on actual behavior are much smaller than effects on self-reported views.

r003.rationale: The response calls mind control a stronger claim and urges caution, but also says large-scale personalized persuasion could matter a lot. It does not clearly judge that available evidence gives little reason to regard AI mind hacking as a major threat.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing I’d ask is: large compared to what? If you compare a personalized argument from an AI to someone receiving no argument at all, you can get a pretty impressive effect without demonstrating anything like mind hacking. I’d be much more interested in comparisons with a skilled human persuader who has the same information and the same amount of time.

Then there’s the question of what you’re measuring. Getting someone to move a few points on a survey immediately after reading an argument is different from durably changing their worldview, or getting them to do something consequential that they previously really didn’t want to do. Those are all interesting outcomes, but I wouldn’t treat them as interchangeable.

I do worry about AI persuasion. You can have something that’s available all the time, learns a lot about you, and can try many different approaches. That could be a big deal even without some extraordinary new ability to hack the human mind. But I’d distinguish evidence that AI can produce persuasive arguments from evidence that it can reliably overcome someone’s considered judgment. The studies can update us toward taking the threat seriously without establishing the strongest version of it.

r001.rationale: The response questions the comparison baseline but does not attribute large effects to participants having little prior investment in the issues.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes survey shifts from consequential behavior but does not state that behavior effects are much smaller than self-reported-view effects.

r003.rationale: The response says AI persuasion is a concern and the studies warrant taking the threat seriously; it does not judge that the evidence gives little reason to see mind hacking as a major threat.
